title: The Ikshvaku Dynasty: The Solar Line from Manu to Rama and Beyond

beats.text: Long before history was written down, poets in ancient India sang of a royal family that claimed descent from the Sun itself. They called it the Solar line.
beats.visual: Golden dawn over the ancient city of Ayodhya on the banks of the Sarayu river, the sun rising behind white palace towers

beats.text: Its most famous son is Rama, hero of the Ramayana. But Rama stands near the end of a very long road of kings stretching back to creation.
beats.visual: Prince Rama with his bow standing on a hill, looking back at a long procession of crowned kings fading into golden mist

beats.text: This is the Ikshvaku dynasty, named after the first king of Ayodhya. Today we walk that road, generation by generation.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: Our main guide is the oldest telling, Valmiki's Ramayana, where the royal priest Vasishtha recites the family line not once, but twice.
beats.visual: The white-bearded sage Vasishtha reciting from memory in a royal court, kings and courtiers listening intently

beats.text: We will also hear from the Puranas, the poet Kalidasa, and Buddhist and Jain traditions. When they differ, we will say so.
beats.visual: An ancient library with palm-leaf manuscripts spread on a low wooden table, oil lamps glowing softly

beats.text: Here is the family tree we will follow, drawn mostly from Valmiki's list. Watch it grow as our story moves down the ages.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Brahma

chapters.title: From the Creator to the Sun

beats.text: Vasishtha begins at the very beginning. In his second recitation, water covers everything, the self-born Brahma appears, and as a boar he raises the earth.
beats.visual: An endless cosmic ocean under a starry sky, the four-faced god Brahma appearing in radiant light above the waters, a great divine boar lifting the earth from the sea

beats.text: From Brahma came the sage Marichi, and from Marichi came Kashyapa, a father of gods and of countless creatures.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Marichi,Kashyapa

beats.text: Kashyapa's son was Vivasvan, a name of the Sun god himself. This link gives the family its title, the Suryavamsha, the Solar dynasty.
beats.visual: Surya the Sun god riding a golden chariot drawn by seven horses across a blazing sky, the sage Kashyapa watching from a mountaintop

beats.text: And the Sun's son was Vaivasvata Manu, whom Valmiki calls Prajapati, a lord of creatures and the father of humankind.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Vivasvan,Vaivasvata Manu

beats.text: Texts both ancient and later tell of Manu and a great flood. A small fish begs Manu for protection, grows enormous, and warns him of a coming deluge.
beats.visual: Manu building a large wooden ship on a shore while an enormous horned fish rises from the sea

beats.text: When the waters rise, Manu ties his ship to the fish's horn and is carried to a northern mountain. The Puranas say the fish was Vishnu, as Matsya.
beats.visual: A wooden ship roped to the horn of a giant golden fish, sailing through stormy flood waters toward a snowy mountain peak

beats.text: The oldest version, in the Shatapatha Brahmana, does not yet name the fish as Vishnu. Either way, Manu survives to begin the human story anew.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

chapters.title: Ikshvaku and the Founding of Ayodhya

beats.text: Manu's son was Ikshvaku. Valmiki calls him, simply and proudly, the first king of Ayodhya.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Ikshvaku

beats.text: In Valmiki's words, this world was first conferred upon Ikshvaku by Manu. The father hands the earth to his son.
beats.visual: Manu placing a golden crown on young Ikshvaku's head beside the Sarayu river, a new city rising behind them

beats.text: The Puranas add a curious birth story. Ikshvaku, they say, was born from Manu's sneeze, kshut in Sanskrit, and was the eldest of Manu's sons.
beats.visual: Manu seated in a forest hermitage, a radiant infant appearing before him in a soft burst of light

beats.text: A popular explanation links his name to ikshu, sugarcane. That comes from folk and Jain tradition, not settled fact.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: His city, Ayodhya, means the one that cannot be conquered. It became the heart of the kingdom of Kosala, on the banks of the Sarayu.
beats.visual: Panoramic view of ancient Ayodhya with white palaces, gardens and stone steps along the Sarayu river at golden hour

beats.text: Valmiki's last book says Ikshvaku had many sons. The twelfth, Nimi, founded another royal house, the Janakas of Mithila.
beats.visual: King Ikshvaku on his throne surrounded by many young sons, one son, Nimi, bowing as he departs for a distant land

beats.text: So Janaka's family and Rama's family would be distant cousins. Keep that in mind. It will matter at a royal wedding.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: After Ikshvaku, Valmiki lists Kukshi, then Vikukshi. The Puranas call Vikukshi Ikshvaku's eldest son, and tell a story about him.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Kukshi,Vikukshi

beats.text: Ikshvaku sent Prince Vikukshi to the forest to gather food for a rite honoring the ancestors. On the way home, the hungry prince ate a hare.
beats.visual: Young Prince Vikukshi resting under a tree in a forest at dusk, a hunting bow beside him, looking guilty

beats.text: The offering was spoiled, and Ikshvaku sent his son away. Vikukshi became known as Shashada, the hare eater, though he later returned to rule.
beats.visual: The sage Vasishtha pointing gravely at a basket of offerings while King Ikshvaku turns away from his son Vikukshi

beats.text: The Puranas say Vikukshi's son, Puranjaya, helped the gods against the asuras, but would only ride into battle on Indra himself.
beats.visual: Prince Puranjaya in golden armor speaking to the god Indra among the clouds, gods gathered behind them

beats.text: So Indra became a great bull, and Puranjaya rode upon its hump, its kakud. He was called Kakutstha, the one who stands on the hump.
beats.visual: The warrior prince Kakutstha riding atop a giant white divine bull through the clouds, bow raised high

beats.text: Later tradition says Rama is called Kakutstha after this ancestor. Yet Valmiki names the Kakutsthas after Bhagiratha's son, Kakutstha. Here the sources disagree.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

chapters.title: Mandhata, Lord of the Whole Earth

beats.text: Valmiki's list then runs Bana, Anaranya, Prithu, Trishanku, Dhundhumara, Yuvanashva and Mandhata. The Puranas place Trishanku much later.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Bana,Anaranya,Prithu,Trishanku,Dhundhumara,Yuvanashva,Mandhata

beats.text: The Puranas say King Yuvanashva had no son. During a rite in a hermitage, he drank by mistake the blessed water meant for his queen.
beats.visual: King Yuvanashva at night in a forest hermitage, drinking from a sacred water pot while sages sleep nearby

beats.text: Wondrously, the child was born from the king's own side. When the baby cried for milk, Indra offered him his own finger to drink from.
beats.visual: The god Indra kneeling gently over a glowing newborn baby in a palace chamber, offering his finger

beats.text: Indra said, he will drink from me. In Sanskrit, mam dhasyati. And so the child was named Mandhata.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: Mandhata grew into a universal ruler. An old verse says that from where the sun rises to where it sets, all the land was Mandhata's.
beats.visual: Emperor Mandhata on a palace balcony, the sun rising on one horizon and setting on the other over a vast kingdom

beats.text: After Mandhata come Susandhi, Dhruvasandhi, a king named Bharata, and then Asita. Hold on to Asita. His troubles will lead us to Sagara.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Susandhi,Dhruvasandhi,Bharata,Asita

beats.text: But first, Trishanku. Valmiki says he longed to enter heaven in his own body. Vasishtha refused, and Vasishtha's angry sons cursed him to become an outcaste.
beats.visual: King Trishanku kneeling before stern young sages in a hermitage, his royal garments turning dark and rough

beats.text: The great sage Vishwamitra took pity on him. When the gods would not attend his rite, Vishwamitra lifted Trishanku toward heaven by his own power.
beats.visual: Sage Vishwamitra with arms raised beside a fire altar, King Trishanku rising into the sky on a beam of light

beats.text: Indra sent him back, and Trishanku tumbled head first, calling out for help. Vishwamitra called, stay! And the king stopped in midair.
beats.visual: Trishanku tumbling upside down through the night sky, Indra at heaven's gate above, Vishwamitra below with outstretched hand

beats.text: In his anger, Vishwamitra created new stars and seven new sages in the southern sky. He even began to create new gods.
beats.visual: Vishwamitra conjuring a glittering new constellation in the southern night sky, stars swirling from his hands

beats.text: At last, a compromise. Trishanku would shine among those stars, head downward, between earth and heaven. Trishanku's heaven still means a place caught in between.
beats.visual: King Trishanku glowing among the stars, suspended between earth and a shimmering second heaven created by the sage Vishwamitra

beats.text: The Puranas give Trishanku a famous son, Harishchandra, the very model of truthfulness. Valmiki's list does not include him at all.
beats.visual: King Harishchandra on his throne, serene and dignified, handing his crown to the sage Vishwamitra

beats.text: To keep a promise to Vishwamitra, the Markandeya Purana says, he gave up his kingdom, parted from his wife and son, and worked as a humble keeper of the riverside ghats.
beats.visual: Harishchandra in humble clothes keeping watch at a riverside ghat at dusk, gentle smoke rising from distant lamps

beats.text: Through every sorrow he kept his word. At last the gods restored everything to him, and he rose to heaven.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: Now back to Asita. Enemy clans, the Haihayas, Talajanghas and Shashabindus, drove him from his kingdom into the Himalayas.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Asita

beats.text: His queen Kalindi was expecting a child. A jealous co-wife slipped her a bitter potion to stop the birth, but the sage Chyavana promised Kalindi a mighty son.
beats.visual: Queen Kalindi bowing before the sage Chyavana in a snowy Himalayan hermitage, the sage blessing her

beats.text: The boy was born together with that bitter potion, sa gara, meaning with gara, so he was named Sagara. One recitation says Asita passed away in exile. The other says he became an ascetic.
beats.visual: Newborn Prince Sagara held up by his mother in a mountain hut, a broken clay vial lying harmless on the floor

beats.text: The Puranas say Sagara grew up to win back his family's throne. Valmiki gives him two queens, Keshini of Vidarbha and Sumati, Garuda's sister.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Sagara

beats.text: The sage Bhrigu granted a boon. Keshini bore one heir, Asamanja. Sumati bore a gourd that gave sixty thousand sons, raised in jars of ghee.
beats.visual: A palace nursery with endless rows of golden jars glowing softly, attendants tending them by lamplight

beats.text: Asamanja behaved so badly that he was sent away. But his son Anshuman was gentle and well loved, and stayed with his grandfather.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Asamanja,Anshuman

beats.text: Sagara held a great horse ritual, the ashvamedha. The royal horse vanished. His sixty thousand sons dug deep into the earth to find it.
beats.visual: Thousands of princes digging into the earth with spades, a vast chasm opening before them, torches glowing

beats.text: Deep below, they found the horse beside the sage Kapila and accused him of theft. Valmiki says Kapila was Vishnu himself, and his blazing glance left only ashes where they stood.
beats.visual: The sage Kapila meditating serenely in an underground glade, a white horse grazing nearby, a wave of radiant light spreading outward

beats.text: Valmiki himself says Indra, disguised as a demon, had stolen the horse to spoil the rite. And tradition links the ocean's name, sagara, to their great digging.
beats.visual: The god Indra in disguise leading away a white royal horse into the shadows, while sixty thousand princes dig deep channels toward the sea

beats.text: Young Anshuman followed the tunnel and found the horse and his uncles' ashes. Garuda told him only the Ganga could free them, and he took the horse home for Sagara's rite.
beats.visual: Prince Anshuman in a vast underground cavern beside a white horse, the great eagle Garuda alighting before him

beats.text: Anshuman tried to bring the heavenly river down, and failed. His son Dilipa tried too, and passed away still searching for a way.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Anshuman,Dilipa

beats.text: Then came Bhagiratha. He performed austerities for a thousand years, until Brahma granted his wish, warning that only Shiva could bear the Ganga's fall.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Bhagiratha

beats.text: So Bhagiratha worshipped Shiva for a year, standing on one toe. And Shiva agreed to receive the river.
beats.visual: King Bhagiratha balancing on one toe atop a Himalayan peak, Shiva appearing above with matted hair and a crescent moon

beats.text: Proud Ganga plunged from heaven, meaning to sweep Shiva away. Instead she was caught, and lost for years, in his matted locks.
beats.visual: The goddess Ganga as a vast cascade of white water pouring from the clouds into the flowing hair of Shiva on Mount Kailash

beats.text: Then Shiva released her in seven streams. One followed Bhagiratha's chariot across the land, while gods and sages watched in wonder.
beats.visual: King Bhagiratha riding a chariot across green plains, a shining river following behind him, gods watching from the clouds

beats.text: At last the Ganga reached the depths and washed over the ashes. The sixty thousand sons of Sagara rose to heaven.
beats.visual: Countless glowing spirits of the sons of Sagara rising from the shimmering river Ganga into a golden sky

beats.text: Brahma named her Bhagirathi, daughter of Bhagiratha. In India, a Bhagiratha effort still means a heroic labor.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

chapters.title: Two Dilipas and the Great Raghu

beats.text: In Valmiki's list, Bhagiratha's son is Kakutstha, and Kakutstha's son is Raghu. Valmiki says the Raghavas are named after this Raghu.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Kakutstha,Raghu

beats.text: But Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha tells it differently. His King Dilipa has no son, and Vasishtha tells him to serve Nandini, daughter of the divine cow Surabhi.
beats.visual: King Dilipa and his queen bowing before the sage Vasishtha in a forest hermitage, a radiant white cow nearby

beats.text: For twenty one days, Dilipa follows Nandini through the forest. Then a lion appears and holds her fast.
beats.visual: King Dilipa walking behind the white cow Nandini through a sunlit forest, a lion emerging from the undergrowth

beats.text: Dilipa offers himself in her place. The lion vanishes, an illusion Nandini raised to test him, and she blesses the king with a son: Raghu.
beats.visual: King Dilipa kneeling with head bowed before a lion, the cow Nandini glowing, the lion dissolving into light

beats.text: So there are two Dilipas. Valmiki's is Bhagiratha's father. Kalidasa's is Raghu's father, just four generations before Rama.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: Kalidasa's Raghu wins every direction, then gives all his wealth away. When the scholar Kautsa needs gold for his teacher, gold rains into Raghu's empty treasury.
beats.visual: Gold coins raining from the night sky into a palace courtyard, King Raghu and the young scholar Kautsa looking on in wonder

beats.text: Valmiki's line runs on from Raghu through Kalmashapada, a king who Valmiki says fell into fearsome ways, then Shankhana, Sudarshana and Agnivarna.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Kalmashapada,Shankhana,Sudarshana,Agnivarna

beats.text: Vasishtha recites them in one long breath, as a family priest would, because every name was proof of an unbroken line.
beats.visual: The sage Vasishtha reciting before a hall of kings, painted portraits of ancestors lining the wall behind him

beats.text: Then Shighraga, Maru, Prashushruka, Ambarisha, Nahusha, Yayati and Nabhaga. Nahusha and Yayati usually belong to the Lunar dynasty, a puzzle for scholars.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Shighraga,Maru,Prashushruka,Ambarisha,Nahusha,Yayati,Nabhaga

beats.text: Then comes Aja. In Valmiki, he is Nabhaga's son. In Kalidasa and most Puranas, he is Raghu's son. Either way, he is Dasharatha's father.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Aja

beats.text: Kalidasa tells his love story. At her bridal choice ceremony, Princess Indumati of Vidarbha walked past many kings and placed her garland on Aja.
beats.visual: Princess Indumati placing a flower garland around Prince Aja's neck in a grand hall of seated kings

beats.text: Years later, a heavenly garland fell from the sage Narada's vina onto Indumati, and she passed away, a celestial nymph released from a curse.
beats.visual: A garland of heavenly flowers drifting down toward Queen Indumati in a palace garden, the sage Narada passing far above with his vina

beats.text: Aja's lament for her is among the most celebrated passages in Sanskrit poetry. He raised their son, then left this world to rejoin her.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: Their son was Dasharatha, king of Ayodhya. And Valmiki says that he, too, had no heir for many years.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Dasharatha

beats.text: He performed the great horse ritual and a rite for sons. From the fire rose a radiant being bearing a bowl of divine rice pudding.
beats.visual: King Dasharatha before a great fire altar, a radiant divine figure rising from the flames holding a golden bowl

beats.text: He shared it among his queens Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra, and four sons were born: Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.
beats.visual: Queens Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra holding newborn babies, Sumitra cradling twins, King Dasharatha beaming with joy

beats.text: But Dasharatha had once promised Queen Kaikeyi two boons. She asked that her son Bharata be crowned, and Rama sent to the forest for fourteen years.
beats.visual: Queen Kaikeyi standing firm in a dim palace chamber as King Dasharatha sits grief-stricken on the floor

beats.text: Bound by his word, Dasharatha agreed, and soon passed away from grief. Like Harishchandra, he chose truth over everything.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: And so we reach Rama, the eldest son, the prince every recitation was leading toward.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Rama

beats.text: In the first recitation, Vasishtha speaks at Mithila, as Rama and Lakshmana are to marry the daughters of King Janaka. Janaka answers with his own family line.
beats.visual: Wedding talks in King Janaka's hall at Mithila, Vasishtha speaking, Dasharatha, Rama and Lakshmana seated, Janaka listening

beats.text: Like brides for like bridegrooms, Vasishtha says. Two noble families show they are equals, and both, remember, trace back to Ikshvaku.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: The second recitation comes at Chitrakuta. Bharata has come to bring Rama home, and Vasishtha recites the line again, this time to Rama himself.
beats.visual: Rama in bark garments in a forest clearing at Chitrakuta, Bharata kneeling before him, the sage Vasishtha speaking, mountains behind

beats.text: Among the Ikshvakus, he says, the first born becomes the sovereign. The kingdom is yours. But Rama will not break his father's word.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: So Bharata returns and rules as regent from the village of Nandigrama, with Rama's sandals enthroned, until his brother comes home.
beats.visual: Bharata in simple robes in a village hall at Nandigrama, reverently placing a pair of wooden sandals on a modest throne

beats.text: Rama's twin sons were Kusha and Lava. Valmiki says Rama gave Kusha the city of Kushavati near the Vindhyas, and Lava Shravasti in the north.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Kusha,Lava

beats.text: Kalidasa adds a haunting scene. The goddess of abandoned Ayodhya appears to Kusha at night, and he moves his capital back to restore the old city.
beats.visual: A sorrowful goddess in faded silks appearing at night in King Kusha's chamber, moonlit empty streets of Ayodhya outside

beats.text: Kusha's son Atithi becomes an ideal king, and Kalidasa races through about twenty one more rulers after him.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Atithi

beats.text: Among these later kings is Hiranyanabha, remembered in the Puranas as a master of yoga and a teacher of the sage Yajnavalkya.
beats.visual: King Hiranyanabha seated in meditation in a palace garden, a young sage Yajnavalkya listening respectfully

beats.text: Kalidasa ends with another Agnivarna, a pleasure-loving king who left the government to his ministers, and then fell ill.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting the later Agnivarna of the Raghuvamsha

beats.text: His queen, who is expecting a child, is crowned to rule for the unborn heir, and the poem simply stops. Scholars still debate whether Kalidasa meant it to end there.
beats.visual: A dignified queen seated alone on the throne of Ayodhya, ministers bowing before her, an unfinished palm-leaf manuscript in the foreground

beats.text: The Puranas say a King Maru of this line lives on through yoga in the Himalayan village of Kalapa, waiting to renew the Solar line in a future age.
beats.visual: King Maru, an ancient king, meditating in a snowy Himalayan village of stone huts, soft mountain light around him

beats.text: The Puranas carry the line on to Brihadbala, king of Kosala, who sided with the Kauravas at Kurukshetra, where his story ended before Arjuna's son Abhimanyu.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Brihadbala

beats.text: They name the last king as Sumitra, in the age of Kali. Before him come Shuddhodana, the Buddha's father, and a Prasenajit. Here real royal families were likely woven in.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic highlighting Sumitra

beats.text: The Buddha's link to this family runs deep. In Buddhist texts, his own Shakya clan descends from King Okkaka, the Pali form of Ikshvaku.
beats.visual: The ancient town of Kapilavastu at the foot of the Himalayas, Shakya nobles gathered in a teak grove

beats.text: The Buddha himself is called Adiccabandhu, kinsman of the Sun. A prince of the Solar line became a teacher of awakening.
beats.visual: Same as previous picture

beats.text: In Jain tradition, the Ikshvaku clan begins with Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara, whose clan name is linked with sugarcane offered to him as a child.
beats.visual: The infant Rishabhanatha reaching for a stalk of sugarcane offered by Indra in a celestial court

beats.text: Jain sources count most of the twenty four Tirthankaras as Ikshvakus, though the exact count varies. And Jain Ramayanas make Rama an Ikshvaku too.
beats.visual: Serene Jain Tirthankara statues carved in white marble inside a candlelit temple, devotees offering flowers

beats.text: History adds its own echo. In the third century, a real dynasty calling itself the Ikshvakus ruled in Andhra, at Nagarjunakonda, and its queens supported Buddhism.
beats.visual: An ancient Buddhist stupa and monastery at Nagarjunakonda by the Krishna river, royal women offering flowers

beats.text: Whether they truly descended from the epic kings, no one can prove. Later Rajput clans also claimed descent from Kusha and Lava, as family tradition.
beats.visual: Rajput warrior-kings in a desert fort at sunset, honoring a painted royal family tree that traces back to Kusha and Lava

beats.text: And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says he taught eternal yoga to the Sun, who taught it to Manu, who taught it to Ikshvaku.
beats.visual: Krishna on a chariot at dawn at Kurukshetra, a vision of Surya, Manu and Ikshvaku glowing in the sky behind him

beats.text: Step back, and the whole tree comes into view: from the creator, through the Sun and Manu, to Ikshvaku, Sagara, Bhagiratha, Raghu and Rama.
beats.visual: Animated family tree graphic, whole tree visible, highlighting the great kings

beats.text: The lists do not agree. From Ikshvaku to Rama, Valmiki counts about thirty five generations, the Puranas roughly sixty. But every version keeps the same heart: kings bound by their word.
beats.visual: The aged sage Vasishtha seated at sunset by the Sarayu river, palm-leaf manuscripts beside him

beats.text: That is the true inheritance of the Ikshvakus. Not a crown, but a promise kept. Thank you for walking the Solar line with us.
beats.visual: The sun setting over Ayodhya and the Sarayu, a single oil lamp floating on the golden water

sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 38-44 (Sagara, Bhagiratha and the Ganga), 57-62 (Trishanku, Shunahshepa), 66 (Sita found in the furrow), 70-71 (Vasishtha's genealogy at Mithila; Janaka's reply), Dutt translation
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 110 (second genealogy at Chitrakuta; first-born rule), 115 (Bharata rules from Nandigrama), Dutt translation
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 56-57 (Nimi, Videha branch), 107-108 (Kusha at Kushavati, Lava at Shravasti)
Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha cantos 1-8 (Dilipa, Nandini, Raghu, Kautsa, Aja and Indumati) and 15-19 (Kusha, Atithi, later kings, Agnivarna)
Vishnu Purana 4.1-4.4, 4.22, 4.24 (Ikshvaku's birth, Vikukshi, Puranjaya-Kakutstha, Mandhata, Sagara's reconquest, Hiranyanabha, Maru, Brihadbala, future kings)
Bhagavata Purana 8.24 (Matsya), 9.6-9.12 (Solar dynasty; Sumitra as the last king)
Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Manu and the flood); Aitareya Brahmana 7.13-18 (Shunahshepa)
Bhagavad Gita 4.1 (yoga taught to Vivasvan, Manu, Ikshvaku)
Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Brihadbala of Kosala at Kurukshetra)
Digha Nikaya 3, Ambattha Sutta (Okkaka and the Shakyas); Sutta Nipata 3.1 (Adicca clan; Adiccabandhu)
Jain tradition: Jinasena's Adipurana, Kalpa Sutra (Rishabhanatha and the Ikshvaku clan); Vimalasuri's Paumachariya
Nagarjunakonda inscriptions (historical Ikshvakus of Andhra, third century CE)
Rajput bardic genealogies and Tod's Annals of Rajasthan (claimed descent from Kusha and Lava; low confidence, presented as tradition)
